85.title: The ten plagues (Exodus 7–10)
85.hook: blood, frogs, lice, swarms, pestilence, boils, hail, locusts, darkness
85.carry: ten ways to say let go
85.howItsDone: At the Passover seder, as the ten plagues are read, many Jews remove a drop of wine from their cup for each one, and recite Rabbi Judah's three-word memory code.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kotzer ruach, shortness of breath: the first demand, and the bricks got harder to make. Your line was it gets harder first. Today, the blows begin.

At a Passover seder, there's a moment when someone reads out a list. At each word, people at many tables dip a finger in their wine and let a drop fall onto a plate. Blood. Frogs. Lice. Wild beasts. Pestilence. Boils. Hail. Locusts. Darkness. The death of the firstborn. Ten drops. In some homes, there are even toy frogs. Then someone reads a strange line: Rabbi Judah used to make them into a code, three nonsense words from their first letters, detzach, adash, be'achav, so he could remember them.
screen: `TEN DROPS OF WINE.` → `BLOOD, FROGS, LICE…` → `DETZACH, ADASH, BE'ACHAV.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word is makot: blows, strikes. The Torah also calls them signs and wonders. They come in a rhythm. Moses warns Pharaoh; Pharaoh refuses; the blow falls; Pharaoh begs and promises, and when it lifts, changes his mind. Again and again. They start with the Nile, Egypt's lifeline, and the river where Hebrew babies were thrown. It turns to blood. Then frogs come up out of it, into bedrooms and ovens and kneading bowls. Then lice from the dust. At the third plague, Pharaoh's own magicians, who copied the first two, give up: "This is the finger of God." Then swarms of wild creatures, and something new begins: the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, is set apart; the plague doesn't touch it. Then pestilence on the livestock, boils, hail with fire running through it, locusts that eat everything the hail left. Then darkness, so thick that "they saw not one another" for three days. But the Israelites, the text says, had light where they lived. Why so many? The Torah gives more than one reason. On the last night, God says, "against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments." Some readers match the plagues to powers Egypt held divine, like the Nile and the sun. Some rabbis added another reading: every plague was a chance for Pharaoh to change. Ten warnings, the same message louder each time. Let them go.

segments.voice: The seder says every generation should see itself as if it had gone out of Egypt. So name one thing that holds people in a narrow place now, for someone else or for yourself: debt, addiction, loneliness, injustice, fear, a phone that won't let go. You don't have to fix it; just see it clearly, the way you'd see a plague.
Makot. Blows, strikes, plagues. The ten blows on Egypt, each one saying the same thing: let my people go.
Your line: ten ways to say let go. Each blow came with a warning first. Day eighty-five, done.

86.title: Pharaoh's hard heart (Exodus 8–10)
86.hook: each time he relents, then hardens; the rabbis say a heart can harden by habit
86.howItsDone: Jewish tradition uses Pharaoh's hardening to teach about teshuvah, turning back, and about how small repeated choices shape character; Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the fathers, is often studied on Shabbat afternoons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, makot: ten blows, each one a warning. Your line was ten ways to say let go. Today, the question everyone asks about those plagues: why didn't Pharaoh just listen?

Some people can't back down. The argument is lost, everyone can see it, and still: no. Or the promise to change, made in the middle of a crisis, gone the moment things calm down. Frogs are everywhere, in Pharaoh's bed, in his ovens. He calls Moses in a panic: pray for me, take them away, and I'll let the people go. Moses prays, and the frogs die. And the text says: when Pharaoh saw there was relief, he hardened his heart.
screen: `THE PROMISE MADE IN A CRISIS.` → `PRAY FOR ME, I'LL LET THEM GO.` → `RELIEF, AND A HARD HEART.`

segments.voice: Read the plagues closely and you'll notice a pattern in the language. In the early plagues, the Torah says Pharaoh's heart was hardened, or Pharaoh hardened his heart. No one else is named as doing it. After the blood: "and Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he hearkened not unto them." After the frogs, the lice, the swarms, the pestilence: the same. Then, at the sixth plague, the boils, the language turns: "And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh." From then on, it's mostly God who hardens it. That's troubling. If God hardened his heart, was Pharaoh still choosing? The rabbis argued about it, and gave different answers. Maimonides said Pharaoh sinned freely at first, so badly and so often that he lost the path back: the door of turning closed, as a consequence of his own choices. Sforno, a later Italian commentator, said nearly the opposite: God strengthened Pharaoh's heart so he could choose freely, and not just give in because of the pain. Either way, notice the first five times: the text names no one forcing him. Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the fathers, has a line that fits: one wrong deed drags another after it. Every time he said no, the next no came easier. Hebrew uses three words for this hardening: chazak, strong, the same word as chazak at the end of Genesis; kaved, heavy; and kasheh, hard. A heart can get strong in the wrong way, heavy, stiff. The rabbis' lesson is simple and a little scary: hearts harden by habit.

segments.voice: Think of a position you keep repeating, with a person or an idea, mostly because you've always said it: a grudge, an I'll never, an old argument with a family member. Put your hand on your chest if you like, and ask: is this still true, or just a habit? You don't have to give it up; just loosen your grip a little.
Lev, Hebrew for heart, the place of thought and choice, not only feeling. He promises, then hardens, again and again, until the hardening becomes who he is.
Your line: hearts harden by habit. Small choices, repeated, shape a heart. Eighty-six days, and counting.

87.title: The night of the firstborn (Exodus 11–12)
87.hook: blood on the doorposts, and the Lord passes over the houses
87.tomorrow: bread with no time to rise
87.howItsDone: Every spring Jews hold a Passover seder at home, retelling the Exodus from the Haggadah; a child asks why this night is different, and the family eats matzah and bitter herbs and tells the story in answer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lev, every promise forgotten the moment relief came. Your line was hearts harden by habit. Now, the last plague, and the night that became a holiday.

Every spring, at a table full of family, the youngest child who can read stands up, sometimes nervous, sometimes showing off, and sings a question. Ma nishtanah halailah hazeh mikol haleilot? Why is this night different from all other nights? Why the flat bread? Why the bitter herbs? Why do we dip, and lean? The whole long evening that follows is the answer. It's called the seder, and it retells one night.
screen: `THE YOUNGEST CHILD STANDS UP.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?` → `THE WHOLE EVENING IS THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Moses warns Pharaoh of one final blow: at midnight, every firstborn in Egypt will die. Then God gives the Israelites very specific instructions. Each household takes a lamb. On the fourteenth day of the month, they slaughter it, and with a bunch of hyssop put some of its blood on the two doorposts and the top of the door. They roast it and eat it that night, with flat bread and bitter herbs, dressed for travel, shoes on, staff in hand, in a hurry. No one is to go out of the house until morning. God says: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you." That's Pesach, from a Hebrew root that means to pass over, or, some say, to hover over, protecting. At midnight it happens. There's a great cry in Egypt, the text says, for there was not a house where there was not one dead. It's a terrible night. The Torah doesn't hide it, and Jewish tradition doesn't treat it as simple; the spilled wine and the silenced angels come later this week. And before anyone has even left, God tells them to make this night a memorial forever. The Torah says your children will ask: "What mean ye by this service?" And the commandment is: "And thou shalt tell thy son in that day." That's why a child asks the questions at the seder. Freedom isn't only something that happened. It's something you tell, out loud, to the next person, every year.
screen: `A LAMB, BLOOD ON THE DOORPOSTS.` · `PESACH: TO PASS OVER.` · `A GREAT CRY IN EGYPT.` · `AND THOU SHALT TELL THY SON.` · then, large: `THIS NIGHT IS DIFFERENT.`

segments.voice: If you have something small nearby, a piece of bread, a cracker, some fruit, hold it a moment before you eat; if not, just imagine it. Think of something you were brought out of: a hard time, a narrow place, something that once held you. Then eat it slowly, and let it be a small memorial.
Pesach. Passover. The night God passed over the marked houses, and the name of the holiday that retells it every spring.
Your line: this night is different. The answer always starts with a child's question. Until tomorrow.

88.title: Bread with no time to rise (Exodus 12:33–42)
88.hook: dough on their shoulders, and a mixed multitude going with them
88.howItsDone: During the week of Passover Jews eat matzah and remove leavened bread, chametz, from their homes; at the seder the matzah is lifted and called the bread of affliction.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pesach: blood on the doorposts, a terrible midnight, and a child's question every spring. Your line was this night is different. Now it's morning, and it's time to go.

The taxi's downstairs. The flight is in two hours. Somebody is grabbing half-packed bags, leaving dishes in the sink, the bread they meant to bake still sitting in a bowl. After generations in Egypt, it happens to a whole people in one night. Pharaoh, broken, calls Moses and Aaron in the night: get out, all of you, go. The Egyptians push them to hurry. And the dough for tomorrow's bread hasn't risen yet.
screen: `THE TAXI'S DOWNSTAIRS.` → `GET OUT, ALL OF YOU.` → `THE DOUGH HASN'T RISEN.`

segments.voice: The Torah paints it in one detail: "And the people took their dough before it was leavened," their kneading bowls wrapped in their cloaks, on their shoulders. When they stop to eat, they bake the dough into flat cakes, because they "could not tarry." That's matzah: flour and water, baked before it can rise. Every year at Passover, Jews eat it, and many clear leavened bread from their homes for the whole week. Here's the interesting part: matzah means two opposite things at once. Early in the seder, people lift it up and call it the bread of affliction, a phrase from Deuteronomy: the poor bread of slaves. Later the same evening, the Haggadah explains it another way: the bread of freedom, dough that had no time to rise before they were set free. Same bread. It depends on which side of the door you're on. Then a small detail that's easy to miss: "And a mixed multitude went up also with them." Not only the children of Israel. Maybe Egyptians, maybe other slaves, people who had seen what happened and decided to go. The Torah doesn't explain who, and it doesn't turn them away. And the text counts the time: four hundred and thirty years, and on that very day, they went out. It calls that night a night of watching, kept by God, and kept by the people ever after. When the moment came, they didn't wait for the bread to be perfect. They went.

segments.voice: Think of something you've been holding back until it's perfect: a message you keep rewriting, a plan you keep refining, a step you're waiting to feel ready for. Ask yourself whether it's ready enough; flat bread still feeds people. Decide on one thing you'll let go of as it is.
Matzah. Flat bread, baked before it could rise. The bread of affliction, and the bread of freedom.
Your line: go when it's time. Freedom didn't wait for the dough. That's day eighty-eight.

89.title: At the sea (Exodus 14)
89.hook: the army behind, water ahead; midrash says Nachshon walked in first
89.howItsDone: The crossing of the sea is read in synagogue on the seventh day of Passover, the day tradition says it happened, and on the Shabbat of the Song; Nachshon's story is a favorite in Jewish teaching about courage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, matzah: dough on their shoulders, a mixed multitude, and no time to wait. Your line was go when it's time. Now they're out, and trapped.

Freedom lasts about three days before Pharaoh changes his mind. Again. He takes six hundred of his best chariots and gives chase. The Israelites are camped by the sea, and they look up and see the army coming. Water in front. Soldiers behind. Nowhere to go. The people panic, and turn on Moses with one of the most bitter lines in the Torah: "Because there were no graves in Egypt, hast thou taken us away to die in the wilderness?"
screen: `SIX HUNDRED CHARIOTS.` → `WATER AHEAD, SOLDIERS BEHIND.` → `WERE THERE NO GRAVES IN EGYPT?`

segments.voice: Moses answers with calm, famous words: "Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD." It sounds perfect. Then God says something surprising back: "Wherefore criest thou unto Me? speak unto the children of Israel, that they go forward." Why are you crying out to me? Tell them to move. Into the water? Moses lifts his staff, a strong east wind blows all night, the sea splits, "and the waters were a wall unto them on their right hand, and on their left." But the rabbis noticed a gap between go forward and the sea splitting. Who moved first? The Talmud tells a story. The tribes stood at the edge, each saying: I'm not going in first. You go. Then one man, Nachshon, son of Amminadav, a prince of the tribe of Judah, walked into the sea. Up to his ankles. His knees. His waist. His neck. The midrash says the water reached his nostrils, and only then did the sea split. Another opinion in the same passage says the tribe of Benjamin jumped in first, and the Torah itself names no one. But Nachshon's story stuck: in modern Hebrew, a nachshon is someone who goes first, a pioneer. The Israelites walk through on dry ground. The Egyptians follow, and the waters come back over them. The Torah says the people saw, and they believed. But first somebody had to get their feet wet.
screen: `STAND STILL, AND SEE.` · `SPEAK TO THEM, THAT THEY GO FORWARD.` · `NACHSHON WALKS IN.` · `A WALL ON THE RIGHT AND THE LEFT.` · then, large: `WALK IN FIRST.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're standing at the edge of: a hard conversation, an application, a doctor's appointment, a new start. Notice the part of you waiting for the sea to split first, for the fear to go, for a sign, for someone else to go. Then picture the first step, just ankle deep, and see yourself taking it.
Nachshon. The prince of Judah who, the midrash says, walked into the sea first, while the people stood trapped between an army and the water.
Your line: walk in first. In the midrash, the sea split only once someone was in it. Day eighty-nine, done.

90.title: The Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:1–18)
90.hook: the people sing; the rabbis say God hushed the angels because the Egyptians were drowning (Megillah 10b)
90.howItsDone: Jews say the Song of the Sea in the morning prayers, and its line mi chamocha in the evening and morning prayers; at the seder many spill a drop of wine for each plague, and the Song is read in synagogue on the seventh day of Passover.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nachshon walked in up to his nose before the sea split. Your line was walk in first. Now they're on the other side.

A test result that comes back clear. A phone call saying they're safe. The moment the thing chasing you is gone. Now multiply that relief by a whole people, standing on a beach at dawn, soaking wet, looking back at the water where the army was. Generations of slavery, and it's over. What do you do in a moment like that? They sing. And the angels aren't allowed to join in.
screen: `A TEST RESULT THAT COMES BACK CLEAR.` → `A PEOPLE ON A BEACH AT DAWN.` → `THEY SING.`

segments.voice: "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD." It begins: "I will sing unto the LORD, for He is highly exalted; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea." This is Shirat HaYam, the Song of the Sea. In a Torah scroll it's even written differently from the text around it, laid out like bricks in a wall. One line from it, "Who is like unto Thee, O LORD, among the mighty?", in Hebrew mi chamocha, is said in Jewish prayer every single day. Nobody tells the people they were wrong to sing. But the Talmud tells a story about that same moment. Up in heaven, the ministering angels wanted to sing too, and God stopped them. The works of my hands are drowning in the sea, and you want to sing? The Egyptians had enslaved and chased the Israelites. They were still God's creatures. The Talmud adds a subtle line: God doesn't rejoice at the downfall of the wicked, though God may let others rejoice. The people who were just saved can sing. But nobody should throw a party over someone drowning. In the same spirit, at the seder, many people spill a drop of wine for each of the ten plagues. One explanation: a full cup is a sign of joy, and the joy is made a little less, because people suffered. The book of Proverbs says it too: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth." Be grateful you're safe. Sing. Just don't sing over the drowning.

segments.voice: Think of a recent win, something that went your way: an argument, a game, a promotion, a rival who stumbled, and let yourself be really glad about it. Then think of the person on the other side and what it cost them, and hold both at once. If you pray, you can give thanks for what went well.
Mi chamocha, Hebrew for who is like You: a line from the Song said in Jewish prayer every day, sung on the far shore while the angels were told to be quiet.
Your line: don't sing over the drowning. Gratitude can sing without gloating. See you tomorrow.

91.title: Miriam's timbrel (Exodus 15:20–21)
91.hook: the prophetess takes a drum and leads the women in dance
91.howItsDone: Miriam's song is read in synagogue with the Song of the Sea each year, and in many communities women mark it by singing and drumming together, some on the seventh day of Passover.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mi chamocha, and God hushing the angels. Your line was don't sing over the drowning. That ends a week: the plagues, a hard heart, the night of the firstborn, bread with no time to rise, the sea, the song.

A drum is an awkward thing to pack. It's round, it's bulky, and it doesn't feed anybody. The Israelites left Egypt so fast the bread didn't have time to rise. And yet, on the far shore, with the water closed and the people safe, one woman reaches into her bag and pulls out a drum. Then another woman does. And another. Somebody packed the drums.
screen: `A DRUM IS HARD TO PACK.` → `NO TIME FOR THE BREAD TO RISE.` → `SOMEBODY PACKED THE DRUMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances." Three things in one line. First, the title: the Torah itself calls Miriam a prophetess. Why the sister of Aaron, and not of Moses? The Talmud answers with a story: she prophesied when she was only Aaron's sister, before Moses was born, that her mother would have a son who would save the people. Tradition says she's the girl who watched the basket on the Nile. Now she's leading the women in dance. Second, the drum. A timbrel is a hand drum, skin stretched over a frame, held up and struck with the palm. The midrash asks: where did these women get drums, in the desert, after leaving in such a rush? The answer, which Rashi passes on: they were so sure God would do wonders for them that they packed their drums in Egypt. They carried the celebration before there was anything to celebrate. Third, the song. Miriam sings one line back to the women, "Sing ye to the LORD, for He is highly exalted", nearly the line Moses opened with. Moses sings the long song; Miriam gets everyone dancing. Both belong to the story. Some Jewish women today point to this verse when they sing, drum and lead in their own communities. And the lesson inside it is quiet: hope isn't only a feeling. Sometimes it's a thing you put in your bag.
